Key Concepts

Central Tendency

Mean: The arithmetic average — sum of values divided by count
Median: The middle value when data is ordered
Mode: The most frequent value



Variability

Range: Difference between maximum and minimum
Variance: Average of squared deviations from the mean
Standard Deviation: Square root of variance — same units as the data



Distribution Shape

Normal: Symmetric, bell-shaped
Skewed: Asymmetric (positive = tail to right, negative = tail to left)
Bimodal: Two peaks

What Is R?
R is a programming language designed for statistical analysis. It’s:

Free and open-source — anyone can use it
Powerful — handles everything from simple means to complex models
Widely used — the standard in psychology, biology, medicine, and data science
Reproducible — your analysis is documented in code


Why Learn R?
Excel can calculate a mean. So why bother with R?

Reproducibility: R code documents exactly what you did. “I calculated the mean” becomes mean(data$reaction_time) — clear and precise.
Efficiency: Once written, code can be reused. Analyse one dataset, apply the same analysis to another.
Capabilities: R handles analyses that Excel simply cannot — bootstrapping, mixed models, complex visualisations.
Transparency: Sharing code lets others check your work. This is increasingly required in psychology journals.

R Basics for Today
You don’t need to master R today — just understand enough to follow along. Here are the essentials:

Assigning Values
Use <- (less-than followed by dash) to assign values:
# Store a value
my_score <- 75

# Store multiple values
reaction_times <- c(245, 312, 278, 298, 267)
The c() function combines values into a vector (a list of numbers).


Basic Functions
Functions do things. They have a name followed by parentheses containing inputs:
# Mean of values
mean(c(10, 20, 30))

# Sum of values
sum(c(10, 20, 30))

# Number of values
length(c(10, 20, 30))


Computing Descriptives
For descriptive statistics, you’ll use:



Function
What It Does




mean(x)
Arithmetic mean


median(x)
Median (middle value)


sd(x)
Standard deviation


var(x)

Minimum value

Maximum value

Example: Reaction Times
# Create data
rt <- c(245, 312, 278, 298, 267)

# Compute statistics
mean(rt)     # 280
median(rt)   # 278
sd(rt)       # 26.2

Understanding Output
When R gives you output, it includes some formatting. For example:
[1] 280
The [1] just means “first element.” For a single number, you can ignore it.
For longer output:
[1] 245 267 278 298 312
The numbers 245, 267, etc. are your data. The [1] tells you where the first element is.

Working with Data Frames
Real datasets aren’t just vectors — they’re data frames (like a spreadsheet with rows and columns).

Accessing Columns
Use $ to access a column:
# If 'olympics' is your dataset
olympics$reaction_time     # Get the reaction_time column
mean(olympics$reaction_time)  # Mean of that column


Subsetting Data
Get specific parts of your data:
# Filter rows where room is "A"
room_a <- olympics[olympics$room == "A", ]

# Get mean reaction time for Room A only
mean(room_a$reaction_time)

Common Errors (And How to Fix Them)

Error: object ‘x’ not found
Meaning: R doesn’t recognise that name.
Fixes:

Check spelling (R is case-sensitive: Data ≠ data)
Make sure you created the object first
Run all code chunks in order



Error: could not find function “x”
Meaning: R doesn’t recognise that function.
Fixes:

Check spelling
Some functions need packages (we’ll load these for you)



Unexpected symbol error
Meaning: R found something it didn’t expect.
Fixes:

Check for missing commas or parentheses
Make sure quotes match (both " or both ')

Part 2: Interpreting Distributions

Exercise 3: Distribution Shapes
For each scenario, predict the distribution shape:
a) Exam scores on an easy test (most students score 80-100%)






TipShow Answer





Negatively skewed (ceiling effect). Most scores cluster near the top, with a tail toward lower scores.



b) Reaction times to a visual stimulus






TipShow Answer





Positively skewed. There’s a lower bound (can’t be negative or below ~150ms), but no upper bound. Occasional slow responses create a right tail.



c) Heights of adult women






TipShow Answer





Approximately normal (symmetric, bell-shaped). Heights tend to cluster around the average with fewer very short or very tall individuals.





Exercise 4: Mean vs Median
A researcher reports: Mean salary = £52,000; Median salary = £38,000
a) What does this tell you about the distribution?






TipShow Answer





The mean is much higher than the median, indicating positive skew. A few very high salaries pull the mean up.



b) Which measure (mean or median) better represents the “typical” salary? Why?






TipShow Answer





The median (£38,000) better represents the typical salary because it’s not affected by the extreme high values. More than half of workers earn less than the mean.

title: Week 12 Homework
text:
Part 4: Conceptual Questions

Exercise 7: True or False
Mark each statement True or False:
a) The mean is always the best measure of central tendency.






TipShow Answer





False. The median is better for skewed data or when outliers are present.



b) Standard deviation tells you about the shape of the distribution.






TipShow Answer





False. SD tells you about spread/variability, not shape. You need to compare mean and median (or look at a histogram) to assess shape.



c) If the mean is greater than the median, the distribution is positively skewed.






TipShow Answer





True. In a positively skewed distribution, extreme high values pull the mean above the median.



d) Variance is always larger than standard deviation.






TipShow Answer





False. When variance < 1, taking the square root gives a larger SD. For example: Variance = 0.25, SD = 0.5. (However, for most psychological data with variance > 1, this statement would be true.)





Exercise 8: The 68-95-99.7 Rule
Reaction times are normally distributed with Mean = 300ms and SD = 40ms.
a) What range contains approximately 68% of reaction times?






TipShow Answer





Mean ± 1 SD = 300 ± 40 = 260ms to 340ms



b) What range contains approximately 95% of reaction times?






TipShow Answer





Mean ± 2 SD = 300 ± 80 = 220ms to 380ms



c) A participant has a reaction time of 200ms. Is this unusual? Why?






TipShow Answer





Yes, this is unusual. 200ms is (300-200)/40 = 2.5 SDs below the mean. Only about 0.6% of values fall this far from the mean in a normal distribution.

Why Summarise Data?
Imagine you collected reaction times from 100 participants. You now have 100 numbers. What do you do with them?
Raw data is overwhelming. We need ways to:

Compress the data into meaningful summaries
Compare groups or conditions
Communicate findings to others
Prepare for statistical tests

Descriptive statistics provide these summaries without losing essential information about what the data is telling us.

title: Week 12 Reading
section: Central Tendency: Where Is the Centre?
text:
Central Tendency: Where Is the Centre?
Central tendency describes the “typical” or “central” value in a dataset. There are three main measures:

The Mean
The mean is the arithmetic average — add up all values and divide by how many there are.
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]
Where:

\(\bar{x}\) is the mean (pronounced “x-bar”)
\(\sum\) means “sum of”
\(x_i\) represents each individual value
\(n\) is the number of values

Example: Reaction times (in ms): 245, 312, 278, 298, 267
\[\bar{x} = \frac{245 + 312 + 278 + 298 + 267}{5} = \frac{1400}{5} = 280\text{ms}\]
Strengths:

Uses all the data
Mathematically useful for further calculations
Most people understand it

Weaknesses:

Sensitive to extreme values (outliers)
Can be misleading with skewed data



The Median
The median is the middle value when data is arranged in order.
Steps:

Sort values from lowest to highest
Find the middle value
If there’s an even number of values, average the two middle ones

Example: Same reaction times sorted: 245, 267, 278, 298, 312
The median is 278ms (the middle value).
With even numbers: 245, 267, 278, 298, 312, 340
Median = (278 + 298) / 2 = 288ms
Strengths:

Not affected by outliers
Better for skewed distributions
Meaningful for ordinal data

Weaknesses:

Doesn’t use all information
Less useful for calculations



The Mode
The mode is the most frequently occurring value.
Example: Memory scores: 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 9
Mode = 7 (appears three times)
Strengths:

Works with categorical data
Easy to identify
Shows what’s most common

Weaknesses:

May not exist (all values unique)
May have multiple modes (bimodal, multimodal)
Ignores most of the data



When to Use Which?








Measure
Best For
Avoid When




Mean
Normally distributed, continuous data
Outliers present, skewed data


Median
Skewed data, ordinal data
You need mathematical precision


Mode
Categorical data, finding typical category
Continuous data with no repeats









TipRule of Thumb



If mean and median are similar, the data is roughly symmetric. If they differ substantially, the data is likely skewed.

title: Week 12 Reading
section: Variability: How Spread Out Is the Data?
text:
Variability: How Spread Out Is the Data?
Two datasets can have the same mean but look very different:

Dataset A: 48, 49, 50, 51, 52 (Mean = 50)
Dataset B: 10, 30, 50, 70, 90 (Mean = 50)

Variability tells us how spread out the values are around the centre.

Range
The range is the simplest measure: maximum minus minimum.
\[\text{Range} = x_{max} - x_{min}\]
Dataset A: Range = 52 - 48 = 4
Dataset B: Range = 90 - 10 = 80
Strengths: Easy to calculate and understand
Weaknesses: Based on only two values; sensitive to outliers


Variance
Variance measures the average of squared deviations from the mean.
For a sample:
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}\]
Steps:

Find the mean
Subtract the mean from each value (deviation)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by (n-1)

NoteWhy n-1?



We divide by (n-1), not n, because we’re estimating the population variance from a sample. This “degrees of freedom” correction makes our estimate unbiased. You’ll understand this better when we cover inference.




Standard Deviation
The standard deviation is the square root of variance:
\[s = \sqrt{s^2}\]
For our example: SD = √686.5 = 26.2ms
Why take the square root? Variance is in squared units (ms²), which isn’t meaningful. Standard deviation returns to the original units (ms).
Interpreting SD:

Roughly 68% of data falls within 1 SD of the mean
Roughly 95% falls within 2 SDs
Roughly 99.7% falls within 3 SDs

title: Week 12 Reading
text:
Distributions: The Shape of Data
A distribution shows how values are spread across their possible range. We can visualise distributions using histograms or density plots.

The Normal Distribution
The normal distribution (or Gaussian distribution) is symmetric and bell-shaped:

Most values cluster around the mean
Fewer values appear as you move away from the mean
The distribution is perfectly symmetric

Properties of normal distributions:

Mean = Median = Mode (all at the centre)
Defined by just two parameters: mean (location) and SD (spread)
Many natural phenomena approximate normal distributions



Skewed Distributions
Positive skew (right skew): Tail extends to the right

Most values are low, with some very high values
Mean > Median
Example: Income (most people earn moderate amounts; few earn very high)

Negative skew (left skew): Tail extends to the left

Most values are high, with some very low values
Mean < Median
Example: Age at retirement (most retire around 65; some retire much earlier)







TipMemory Aid



The tail points in the direction of the skew. Positive skew = tail pointing to positive (right) side.




Bimodal Distributions
Bimodal distributions have two peaks, suggesting two subgroups in the data.
Example: Reaction times might be bimodal if:

One group understood the task immediately
Another group took longer to learn



Identifying Distribution Shape
To identify shape, look for:

Symmetry: Is there a mirror image around the centre?
Tails: Where do extreme values appear?
Peaks: How many centres are there?

Why Distribution Shape Matters
Distribution shape affects:

Which central tendency to report: Use median for skewed data
Which statistical tests to use: Some tests assume normality
How to interpret the data: Skew suggests something interesting is happening
Outlier detection: What counts as “unusual” depends on the distribution

Reporting Descriptives in APA Format
When writing up results, report descriptives clearly:
Format: (M = value, SD = value)
Examples:

Participants’ simple reaction times were relatively fast (M = 280ms, SD = 26.2ms).


Memory performance was moderate (M = 6.4 words, SD = 1.8).

ImportantAlways Report Both



The mean without SD is incomplete. Always report measures of both central tendency AND variability.

title: Week 11 Lab Reading
text:
What You’ll Be Measuring
DataLab includes six stations measuring different aspects of human cognition and behaviour. Here’s the background on each:

Reaction Time
Reaction time is the interval between a stimulus and your response to it.

Simple reaction time: Respond as fast as possible to a single stimulus
Choice reaction time: Choose between responses based on the stimulus

Research shows that adding choices increases reaction time — a finding known as Hick’s Law (Hick, 1952).






NoteWhy It Matters



Reaction time is one of the most reliable measures in psychology. Your data will show how consistent (or variable) human performance is, even on simple tasks.




Memory
The memory task measures how many items you can hold in working memory.
Miller (1956) famously proposed that we can hold about 7 ± 2 items in short-term memory — the “magical number seven.” Your data will test whether this holds for our class.


Estimation
Estimation tasks reveal systematic biases in human judgement.
People often:

Underestimate large quantities
Overestimate small probabilities
Anchor on initial information

We’ll explore whether group discussion improves or worsens estimation accuracy.


Confidence
Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking.
The confidence task measures how well you know what you know:

Are you overconfident (think you’re right when you’re wrong)?
Are you underconfident (doubt yourself when you’re correct)?
Are you well-calibrated (confidence matches accuracy)?

By the end of this term, you’ll be able to: - Design experiments that can answer research questions - Analyse data using R - Interpret results appropriately - And report findings in professional APA format

SLIDE 3: Why Research Methods?
[Show: Why research methods slide]
Psychology is a science. That means we don’t just have opinions about human behaviour — we test those opinions systematically.
To make credible claims about how people think, feel, and behave, we need: - Systematic observation - Controlled experiments - Statistical analysis - And peer review
This module gives you the tools to do all of this.

SLIDE 6: What Is DataLab?
[Show: DataLab description slide]
DataLab is a series of six cognitive task stations.

SLIDE 7: Why DataLab?
[Show: Table showing how student data maps to topics]
Why do we call it DataLab? Because the data YOU generate becomes our teaching dataset for the entire term.

title: Week 11 Reading
section: You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
text:
You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
Right now, if someone asked you “Does social media cause anxiety?”, you might have an opinion. Everyone has one of those. But psychology isn’t about opinions—it’s about evidence. And evidence doesn’t just land in your lap. Someone has to design a way to gather it, collect it carefully, and work out what it actually shows.
That’s what you’re learning to do. By the end of your degree, you won’t just think social media might cause anxiety—you’ll be able to design a study that could actually test the idea, spot the weaknesses in existing research, and understand why the answer might be more complicated than the headlines suggest.

Think about that for a second… You don’t have to rely on anecdote or opinion anymore. You can create knowledge.

title: Week 11 Reading
text:
You’ll See Through the Nonsense
We’re surrounded by claims about human behaviour. Adverts tell us certain products will make us more confident. Influencers promote supplements that supposedly sharpen your mind. News stories announce that scientists have “proved” all sorts of things about personality, intelligence, or relationships. 9 out of 10 adverts are dubious! (not a real stat!)
Most of these claims are, at best, oversimplified. Many are outright wrong. Understanding research methods gives you the ability to look at a study and ask:

How many people did they actually test?
Could something else explain these results?
Is this finding likely to replicate?

This isn’t just academic scepticism. It’s protection against being manipulated by people who use the language of science without the rigour, without the appropriate ‘methods’.

title: Week 11 Reading
text:
These Skills Travel
Psychology graduates end up in all sorts of places: clinical training, education, marketing, human resources, policy research, user experience design, data analysis, all sorts of entrepreneurial activities I don’t understand. What connects these fields is that they all involve understanding people and making decisions based on evidence. It’s just thinking scientifically.
The ability to gather data systematically, analyse it honestly, and communicate what it means is valuable almost everywhere. It’s also incredibly rare. Many people can express opinions confidently; fewer can actually interrogate those opinions with evidence.

title: Week 11 Reading
text:
And One More Thing
Some of you will genuinely enjoy this. Not everyone, and probably not immediately, but there’s real satisfaction in solving methodological puzzles: working out how to test something that seems untestable, spotting a flaw in an argument, seeing a pattern emerge from data you collected yourself.
I’m not promising you’ll love every moment. But we are promising that this material is worth taking seriously—and that taking it seriously might surprise you.






ImportantThis Week



Since Week 11 has no lecture, watch the preview video and use this reading to prepare for the term ahead. But above all, be curious!








Note



Sophie von Stumm (formerly from Goldsmiths!) and colleagues (2011) sought to identify the best predictors of academic performance. Unsurprisingly perhaps, a person’s intelligence was the best predictor. However, they also found that this was matched by the combined predictive power of effort and intellectual curiosity. They conclude that succeeding in academic fields (such as psychology) is not just a question of being smart and trying hard, it is also about having a hungry mind!

Von Stumm, S., Hell, B., & Chamorro-Premuzic, T. (2011). The hungry mind: Intellectual curiosity is the third pillar of academic performance. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 6, 574-588.

title: Week 11 Reading
text:
Why Do Psychologists Do Research?
Psychology aims to understand human behaviour and mental processes. But how do we move from casual observation to scientific knowledge?

The Problem with Common Sense
We often think we understand human behaviour based on everyday experience - my mum certainly thinks so. But “common sense” has limitations (sorry, mum!):

Hindsight bias: Events seem obvious after they occur (“I knew it all along”)
Confirmation bias: We notice evidence that supports our beliefs and ignore contradicting evidence
Anecdotal evidence: Individual cases can mislead — your friend’s experience isn’t representative of everyone

Consider these “common sense” claims:

“Opposites attract” — But also “Birds of a feather flock together”
“Too many cooks spoil the broth” — But also “Many hands make light work”
“Absence makes the heart grow fonder” — But also “Out of sight, out of mind”

Common sense can justify almost any conclusion. Research methods provide systematic tools to overcome these biases and determine which claims actually hold up under scrutiny.


Why Intuitions About Behaviour Are Often Wrong
Our intuitions fail us for several reasons:

We don’t see our own blind spots — We’re unaware of the biases affecting our judgement
Memory is reconstructive — We misremember events to fit our current beliefs
We overgeneralise from small samples — One or two examples feel like proof
We confuse correlation with causation — Two things happening together doesn’t mean one caused the other

For example, studies consistently show that:

People are poor at predicting what will make them happy
Eyewitness testimony is far less reliable than we assume
“Venting” anger often increases rather than decreases aggression

These findings contradict common intuitions — which is precisely why we need systematic research.

title: Week 11 Reading
text:
What Makes a Claim Scientific?

The Difference Between Opinion and Science
An opinion is a personal belief that may or may not be supported by evidence: > “I think social media makes people unhappy.”
A scientific claim is testable, based on systematic evidence, and open to being proven wrong: > “In a study of 1,000 adults, those who used social media for more than 3 hours daily reported lower life satisfaction scores (M = 5.2) than those who used it less than 1 hour (M = 6.8), t(998) = 4.32, p < .001.”


Four Hallmarks of Scientific Claims


Empirical basis — Based on observable, measurable evidence, not just reasoning or authority
Systematic collection — Data gathered using consistent, documented methods
Falsifiability — The claim could, in principle, be proven wrong by evidence
Transparency — Methods are described clearly enough that others could repeat them




What “Replicable” Means
A finding is replicable if other researchers, following the same procedures, get the same results.
Why does this matter?

A single study might have flaws we don’t notice
Random chance can produce misleading results
Researcher bias might influence findings

When multiple independent teams find the same result, we can be more confident it’s real.






NoteThe Replication Crisis



Psychology has faced a “replication crisis” — many classic findings failed to replicate when researchers tried to repeat them. This has led to better practices: larger samples, pre-registration of hypotheses, and more transparency. You’ll learn about this in Week 17.

title: Week 11 Reading
text:
The Scientific Method
Researchers typically follow these steps:

1. Identify a Question
Start with curiosity. What do you want to understand?

“Do people remember information better if they test themselves rather than just re-reading?”



2. Review Existing Knowledge
What have others already discovered? Build on previous work rather than starting from scratch.


3. Formulate a Hypothesis
Make a specific, testable prediction.

“Students who use self-testing will recall more information after one week than students who re-read the material.”



4. Design a Study
Plan exactly how you’ll test your hypothesis: - Who will you study? - What will you measure? - How will you control for other explanations?


5. Collect Data
Gather observations systematically, following your planned procedures.


6. Analyse Results
Use statistics to determine whether your findings are meaningful or could have occurred by chance.


7. Draw Conclusions
What do your results mean? Do they support your hypothesis? What are the limitations?


8. Report Findings
Share your methods and results so others can evaluate and build on your work.
You’ll work through all these steps in your group project this term.

title: Week 11 Reading
text:
Variables: Things That Vary
A variable is anything that can take different values.

Examples of Variables



Variable
Possible Values




Height
150cm, 165cm, 180cm…


Reaction time
200ms, 350ms, 420ms…


Mood
Happy, sad, anxious, neutral…


Number of words recalled
0, 1, 2, 3… 20


Exam score
0-100





Why Variables Matter
Research is fundamentally about understanding how variables relate to each other:

Does study time affect exam performance?
Does sleep quality predict reaction time?
Is age related to memory capacity?

In DataLab, you’ll measure several variables and see how they differ between people and across conditions.


Types of Variables
Continuous variables can take any value within a range: - Height (175.3cm) - Reaction time (287.4ms) - Temperature (36.8°C)
Categorical variables fall into distinct categories: - Gender (male, female, non-binary) - Experimental condition (control, treatment) - Handedness (left, right, ambidextrous)
Discrete variables are countable whole numbers: - Number of items recalled (7) - Number of errors (3) - Number of children (2)
Understanding variable types helps you choose appropriate statistical analyses — something you’ll learn throughout this module.

title: Week 11 Reading
section: How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour
text:
How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour

Moving Beyond Speculation
Without data, debates about human behaviour often go in circles. Everyone has opinions, but how do we know whose is correct?
Empirical evidence allows us to:

Test competing theories — Instead of arguing, we can design studies to see which prediction holds
Discover unexpected findings — Data often reveals patterns we wouldn’t have predicted
Quantify effects — Not just “X affects Y” but “X increases Y by approximately this much”
Identify boundary conditions — Under what circumstances does a finding hold or not hold?



An Example: Does Punishment Deter Crime?
Common sense might suggest that harsher punishments reduce crime. But what does the evidence show?
Research has found: - Certainty of punishment matters more than severity - Very harsh sentences may actually increase recidivism in some cases - Deterrent effects vary by crime type and offender characteristics
Without systematic data collection, we’d have no way to discover these nuances.

title: Week 11 Reading
text:
Connecting to DataLab

Your Data, Your Learning
In Thursday’s lab, you’ll experience research from both perspectives:

As a participant — completing cognitive tasks
As a tester — administering tasks and recording data

This dual perspective helps you understand:

Why standardised procedures matter (you’ll see what happens when instructions vary)
How measurement introduces variability (the same person gives different responses across trials)
What it feels like to generate data that will be analysed

The data you generate will be used throughout the term. When we discuss distributions in Week 12, we’ll look at the distribution of YOUR reaction times. When we learn about t-tests in Week 14, we’ll compare performance between Room A and Room B. This is your data, and you’ll learn statistics by exploring it.

text:

title: Distributions & Variability
text: Where is the centre?

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Three Measures of Centre



Measure
What It Is
When to Use




Mean
Arithmetic average
Normal data, no outliers


Median
Middle value
Skewed data, outliers


Mode
Most frequent
Categorical data

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
The Mean

Mean (\(\bar{x}\)) = Sum of all values ÷ Number of values

\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Mean: Strengths & Weaknesses


Strengths

Uses all data
Mathematically useful
Widely understood


Weaknesses

Sensitive to outliers
Misleading with skew

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
The Median

Median = The middle value when data is ordered

Steps:

Sort values low → high
Find the middle value
If even n, average the two middle values

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Median: Example
Sorted: 245, 267, 278, 298, 312

The median is 278ms (the middle value)

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Median: With Even Numbers
Sorted: 245, 267, 278, 298, 312, 340

Two middle values: 278 and 298


Median = (278 + 298) / 2 = 288ms

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
The Mode

Mode = The most frequently occurring value

Memory scores: 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 9

Mode = 7 (appears three times)

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Which Measure When?






Quick Rule


If mean ≈ median → data is roughly symmetric
If mean ≠ median → data is likely skewed

title: Distributions & Variability
section: How spread out is the data?
text: How spread out is the data?

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Same Mean, Different Data

Dataset A: 48, 49, 50, 51, 52 → Mean = 50
Dataset B: 10, 30, 50, 70, 90 → Mean = 50


These are very different!
Variability captures this difference.

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
The Range

Range = Maximum − Minimum

Dataset A: 52 − 48 = 4
Dataset B: 90 − 10 = 80







Limitation


Range uses only 2 values — very sensitive to outliers

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Variance

Variance (\(s^2\)) = Average of squared deviations from the mean

\[s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}\]

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Variance: Step by Step
Data: 245, 312, 278, 298, 267 (Mean = 280)

Step 1: Find the mean ✓


Step 2: Subtract mean from each value (deviation)


Step 3: Square each deviation


Step 4: Sum the squared deviations → Divide by (n−1)

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Why n−1?






Degrees of Freedom


We divide by (n−1) because we’re estimating population variance from a sample.
This correction makes our estimate unbiased.
More on this when we cover inference!

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Standard Deviation

Standard Deviation (\(s\)) = Square root of variance

\[s = \sqrt{s^2}\]
SD = √686.5 = 26.2ms

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Why SD Instead of Variance?
Variance is in squared units (ms²)

SD returns to original units (ms)


Much easier to interpret!

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Interpreting SD: The 68-95-99.7 Rule
For normally distributed data:



Within
Percentage

~68%


2 SD of mean
~95%


3 SD of mean
~99.7%

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
What Is a Distribution?
A distribution shows how values are spread across their possible range.
Visualised as:

Histograms
Density plots

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
The Normal Distribution

Normal distribution = Symmetric, bell-shaped curve

Properties:

Mean = Median = Mode
Defined by mean (location) and SD (spread)
Many phenomena approximate this

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Skewed Distributions


Positive Skew

Tail to the right
Mean > Median
Example: Income


Negative Skew

Tail to the left
Mean < Median
Example: Age at death

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Memory Aid for Skew






The Tail Tells the Tale


The tail points in the direction of the skew name.
Positive skew → tail points to positive (right) side

title: Distributions & Variability
text:
Bimodal Distributions
Two peaks = Two subgroups

Example: Reaction times might be bimodal if some participants used a different strategy

The Basic Format

Critical Rule


The mean without SD is incomplete.
Always report both central tendency AND variability.

Key Concepts Preview

The Big Question
How do we go from raw data to meaningful summaries?
When you collected reaction times in DataLab, you generated dozens of individual measurements. This week, we learn how to compress that information into statistics that tell a clear story.


Central Tendency
Where is the “centre” of the data?

Mean: The arithmetic average — add everything up, divide by how many
Median: The middle value when sorted — resistant to outliers
Mode: The most common value — useful for categories



Variability
How spread out is the data?

Range: Maximum minus minimum — simple but limited
Standard deviation: How far, on average, values are from the mean



Distribution Shape
What does the data look like?

Normal: Symmetric, bell-shaped
Skewed: Tail on one side (positive = right, negative = left)
Bimodal: Two peaks
